independent.heading: Start here. You do not need to know the banking words.
independent.welcome: Whether you have always relied on someone else, recently lost support, or simply want more confidence, you can take this one step at a time.
steps: Find out what comes in, what goes out and when bills are due.
Understand the payments on a statement before changing them.
Learn how to ask for help and protect yourself from scams.
independent.note: You can open any lesson in any order. You do not need to enter account numbers, passwords or personal financial details.

university.heading: A few basics before you manage student money.
university.welcome: A funding payment can look large, but some of it may already be needed for rent and bills. This journey helps you see the full picture before spending.
steps: Turn your funding and payment dates into a practical spending plan.
Compare the full cost of accommodation and shared bills.
Understand that an overdraft is borrowing, and know where to find support.
university.note: Check your own award notice and housing agreement. Student finance and housing rules differ across the UK.

bills.heading: Understand the words. Then choose one useful step.
bills.welcome: When money is tight, letters and unfamiliar terms can feel overwhelming. You can look up a word here and open whichever lesson helps with the problem in front of you.
steps: Separate essential living costs from money that is already overdue.
Prepare for a conversation about a bill without promising more than you can afford.
Find free advice and recognise offers that could make things worse.
bills.note: There is no daily target. If a notice has an urgent deadline, get advice now rather than waiting to finish lessons.

first-job.heading: Get to know the money behind your first payslip.
first-job.welcome: Your salary before deductions is not the same as the money paid into your account. Start with these terms, then practise using a payslip and planning around payday.
steps: Find gross pay, deductions and take-home pay on a payslip.
Plan the costs you need to cover before and between paydays.
Understand the difference between accessible savings and a workplace pension.
first-job.note: The amounts in lessons are practice examples, not a calculation of your own tax, pension or entitlement.

terms.meaning: A card linked to your bank account. A payment usually uses money in that account; if it takes you into an overdraft, that part is borrowing.
terms.example: A £20 purchase normally reduces the money available in your account by £20.

terms.meaning: A card that lets you borrow from the card provider. You receive a bill and must repay under its terms. Interest and fees can apply.
terms.example: Spending £20 on a credit card creates £20 to repay. It is not extra income.

terms.meaning: Money paid for borrowing, or money you may earn on savings. The rate, period and account terms determine how it is calculated.
terms.example: In a simplified example, 5% of £100 for one year is £5, ignoring fees, tax and changes in the rate.

terms.meaning: Setting money aside for later. A savings account holds cash, but access rules differ: some allow withdrawals when you want; others restrict them.
terms.example: Money you may need for a repair soon needs a different access plan from money put away for years.

terms.meaning: Putting money into assets, such as shares or bonds, hoping for income or growth. Their value can fall and you can get back less than you put in.
terms.example: An investment worth £100 today might be worth £90 when you need to sell. Growth is not guaranteed.

terms.meaning: An investment where you lend to a government or company under agreed terms. Repayment can fail and its sale price can change. A UK government bond is called a gilt.
terms.example: A bond is a loan to its issuer; a share is a piece of ownership. A bank’s ‘fixed-rate savings bond’ is a different type of product.

terms.meaning: An everyday bank or building society account used to receive money, make payments and pay bills. Check any charges and overdraft terms.
terms.example: Wages or a pension can arrive in the account, and a utility payment can leave it.

terms.term: Balance, credit and debit on a statement
terms.meaning: A balance is the amount shown at a point in time. On a current-account statement, a credit usually means money coming in and a debit money going out. Pending payments can affect what is available.
terms.example: ‘Credit £100’ on a current-account statement does not mean you have taken out a credit card.

terms.meaning: Borrowing through your current account when payments take it below zero. An arranged limit is not your own money. Interest or other consequences depend on the terms.
terms.example: A £200 overdraft balance means you owe £200, before any applicable charges.

terms.meaning: Permission for a company to collect agreed payments from your account. Amounts may change with notice. Ending the instruction does not necessarily end the contract or debt.
terms.example: An energy supplier may collect the payment agreed for your account.

terms.meaning: An instruction you give your bank to send a fixed amount regularly. You set the amount and timing, unlike a company collecting a Direct Debit.
terms.example: You could arrange to transfer £10 to your own savings account each month.

terms.meaning: A budget is a plan for money coming in (income) and money leaving (outgoings). Include regular bills, everyday costs and less frequent expenses.
terms.example: A bill due once a year still belongs in your plan, even when it is not due this month.

terms.meaning: Arrears are payments that are overdue. Priority debts can have particularly serious consequences, such as risks to your home. Categories differ across UK nations; get advice if unsure.
terms.example: The loudest reminder is not necessarily the bill with the most serious consequence.

terms.meaning: Gross pay is earnings before deductions. Net pay is the amount after deductions such as tax. Net pay is also called take-home pay.
terms.example: In a fictional payslip, £1,000 gross minus £150 deductions gives £850 net.

terms.meaning: Money intended for retirement. A workplace pension can include contributions from you and your employer. It is different from cash you can readily use for everyday costs.
terms.example: Check the scheme’s rules and access restrictions before treating pension savings as money you can spend now.

terms.meaning: A share represents part-ownership of a company. A fund pools investors’ money into a collection of assets. Both can lose value; spreading investments does not remove risk.
terms.example: Holding a fund is not the same as holding money in a cash savings account.

terms.meaning: An NS&I savings product that enters eligible holdings into prize draws instead of paying regular interest. A prize is not guaranteed. These are not company investment bonds.
terms.example: A prize-fund rate is not a promise that each saver will earn that percentage.

terms.meaning: Security details used to protect an account or approve an action. Do not read them to an unexpected caller or enter them through a link in an unexpected message.
terms.example: If someone says they need your security code to stop a scam, end the contact and check with your bank independently.
